transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Um… I guess what brings me in is this thing that keeps happening at school. I’m a kindergarten teacher, and I know it probably sounds silly, because balloons are everywhere for birthdays and classroom parties—actually last week someone had these huge decorations near the office, and I was trying to remember if we’d turned in the lunch count—

But the second I spot balloons, even if they’re just across the hallway, my chest tightens and I kind of freeze for a moment. Like I can’t think clearly about what I’m supposed to be doing right then. It’s embarrassing, especially at work.
Do you feel like you're going to pass out or have a heart attack when your chest tightens up like that?

I don’t know… I wouldn’t say heart attack, exactly. Passing out, I’m not sure—like, I get really tense and I sort of want to get away from the balloons, but I don’t sit there thinking, “Oh no, I’m dying,” if that makes sense.

It’s more like my brain just locks onto the balloon. Which is ridiculous, because with five-year-olds you’re supposed to be focused on who needs help with scissors or who spilled paint, not… you know, whether something might pop.
Do you feel like you're having a panic attack when you see the balloons and your chest tightens up?

I don’t know if I’d call it a panic attack, exactly… it’s more immediate than that. Like the second I see balloons at school—even if they’re way down the hall—my chest tightens and I kind of freeze. For a moment I can’t get my thoughts in order, like what I was supposed to be doing with the kids or the classroom stuff.

And then my mind just goes to the balloons. Which is so frustrating, because there’s always something going on in kindergarten—someone needs help with glue sticks, someone’s crying because their tower fell over—and I’m just stuck there for a second trying to get myself moving again.
Have you ever had a particularly scary or traumatic experience involving balloons?

Yes… there was. About seven months ago, we had this children’s art celebration at school—parents came in, there were little displays, the kids were so proud of their paintings, and someone had put up balloons everywhere because, you know, that’s what people do for those things.

One of them burst really close to my face. It was so sudden and loud. I remember I was trying to smile and keep things moving because there were families around, and one of the kids had glitter all over his hands—sorry, that’s not really the point. But yes, that’s when it started, after that balloon popped right near me.
Does the tightness in your chest happen only when you see balloons that you think could pop, or does it happen even when you see balloons that are deflated or clearly not going to pop?

It’s mostly when they look like they could pop. Like if one is stretched really tight, or it’s bobbing around near the kids, I know it’s probably just a decoration, but it doesn’t feel that way in the moment. It feels like it could burst right in my face, even if that’s not really likely.

A sad, half-deflated one on the floor is… not great, but it’s not the same. I mean, unless a child starts squeezing it or something—kids do that, they’ll just grab things and twist them, and then I’m thinking about where everyone is standing instead of, like, the morning craft. But yes, the tightness is more with the ones that seem like they could pop.
Do you feel anxious or have a similar reaction to other loud or sudden noises, not just balloons?

I’m not sure… I mean, loud noises in general aren’t my favorite, but I don’t know that I react the same way. In a classroom there are sudden noises all day—chairs scraping, blocks crashing, someone dropping a metal water bottle, and you sort of get used to it because otherwise you’d never finish circle time.

But with balloons it feels… different. Or at least that’s what I notice more. Like if there’s a sudden bang somewhere else, I might jump, but then I can usually tell myself what it was. With balloons, I think I’m already waiting for it, if that makes sense.

Sorry, I’m not sure if that answers what you meant.
Do you think you would have the same reaction if you knew a balloon was going to be popped on purpose, like in a controlled situation?

I think… honestly, even if I knew it was controlled, I’d still react before I could talk myself through it. Like, what brings me in is that the second I spot balloons at school—even across the hallway—my chest tightens and I sort of freeze for a moment.

It’s embarrassing because I’m supposed to be watching the kids, remembering who needs help with their coat, who left their lunchbox by the cubbies, all of that. But for a second my brain just goes straight to the balloon, and I can’t think clearly about what I’m meant to be doing. So if someone said, “We’re going to pop this now,” I don’t know… I think my body would still get there before my mind did.
Do you think you would react the same way if you saw a picture of a balloon, rather than a real one?

A picture… I don’t think it’s quite the same as a real one. Like if I see a balloon in a worksheet or a party invitation or something, I might notice it and kind of dislike it, but it’s not usually that full-body thing.

What gets me is when I spot actual balloons at school, even from across the hallway. Then my chest tightens right away, and I sort of freeze for a second before I can get back to thinking clearly about what I’m supposed to be doing. Like, even if I’m in the middle of getting the kids lined up or checking backpacks, my attention just snaps to it. A picture doesn’t usually feel like it could burst, I guess.
Do you think you would have the same reaction if you saw a balloon that was specifically designed to not pop, like a balloon made of a special material that can't burst?

I think if it really looked different, maybe I’d be better with it… but if it still looked like a regular balloon, especially one that’s stretched tight or bobbing around near the kids, I don’t know that my body would believe it couldn’t pop.

Like, I can know in my head it’s probably just decoration, or in that case that it’s “safe,” but I’d still be watching it. And then I’d start thinking, what if a child grabs it, or it gets too close to my face, or—sorry, I know that’s not exactly what you asked. It’s just that the fear feels bigger than the actual situation. Even when I know it doesn’t really make sense, it feels like it could burst right there.
Do you think you would have any reaction at all if you were in a room filled with balloons that were all tied off and couldn't possibly pop?

I think I would still have some reaction, yes. Even if you told me they couldn’t pop, just being in a whole room of balloons would probably make me tense up.

It’s like at school—sometimes I only see one from way down the hallway, and right away my chest tightens and I kind of freeze for a second. I’ll be thinking about the kids’ backpacks or snack time or who needs to use the bathroom before recess, and then suddenly I’m not thinking about any of that, I’m just focused on the balloon.

So a whole room full of them… tied off or not, I think my body would react before I could remind myself they were safe.
Would you say that your reaction to balloons is primarily because you're afraid of them popping, or is it also because you just don't like being around them in general?

I think it’s mostly the popping, or the possibility of it. Like, I know if there’s a balloon in the classroom it’s probably just decoration, and the kids are excited because it’s someone’s birthday or whatever, but if it’s stretched tight or bobbing near them, my mind goes straight to, “That could burst right in my face.”

And then I get scared in a way that feels… bigger than what’s actually happening. I don’t think I hate balloons just as objects exactly, but being around them makes me uneasy because I’m waiting for that sudden pop.
Do you think you would have any anxiety or reaction if you were in a situation where you knew for certain that no balloons would be present or mentioned?

I’m not totally sure… I mean, if I knew there wouldn’t be any balloons and nobody was going to talk about them, I think I’d probably be okay? Like, I don’t usually sit around thinking about balloons for no reason.

But then again, sometimes when someone says “no balloons,” I almost start picturing them anyway, which is silly. It’s kind of like when the kids are told not to run and then suddenly everyone is thinking about running. Sorry, that’s probably not what you mean. I guess if they really weren’t there and nothing brought them up, I don’t think I’d have much of a reaction.
Would your reaction to balloons change if you knew that the balloons were filled with a substance that made a much softer sound when they popped, rather than the typical loud noise?

Maybe a little? I mean, if I truly knew it wouldn’t make that sharp pop, I think that might help some.

But honestly, when I see one in the classroom, especially if it’s stretched really tight or kind of bobbing around near the kids, my brain doesn’t really stop and think, “Oh, this one would be quieter.” It just goes straight to, “That could burst right in my face,” and I get scared more than the situation probably calls for.

It’s funny, because the kids don’t care at all—they’ll be waving them around like it’s nothing, and I’m trying to act normal and remind them to keep it away from sharp corners or pencils. So yes, softer would probably make it less bad, but I think I’d still feel on edge just seeing it there.
Do you think you would have a similar reaction to other objects that could potentially make a loud noise, but are not balloons?

Not really in the same way, I don’t think. I mean, I don’t love sudden loud noises in general—who does? Like when a chair scrapes really loudly during circle time, all the kids turn around, and then I lose my train of thought completely.

But with balloons it’s different. I know a balloon in the classroom is probably just decoration, but if I see one stretched tight or bobbing near the children, I feel like it could burst right in my face. And then I get scared in a way that seems bigger than what’s actually happening.

So it’s not just “loud noise” as a category, I guess. It’s more specifically the balloon and the possibility of that pop.
Do you think your fear of balloons is the main thing that's been causing you distress, or are there other things in your life that have been making you feel anxious or overwhelmed?

I think the balloon thing is the main one, honestly. I mean, everyone gets overwhelmed sometimes, especially with a classroom full of little kids and someone spilling paint or crying because their shoe feels “wrong”—that happens all the time.

But this feels different. Like, I know a balloon in the classroom is probably just decoration, or for a birthday or whatever, but when I see one stretched tight or bobbing around near the children, it feels like it could burst right in my face. And then I get scared in a way that feels… bigger than the situation, if that makes sense.

So yes, I’d say the balloons are the thing that really sets me off more than anything else.
Has your fear of balloons affected your relationships with your students, colleagues, or family members?

Yeah… I think it has, mostly at work. I try not to let it show with the kids, because they’re little and they get so excited about birthdays and class celebrations, and I don’t want to be the teacher who ruins that. I mean, they already get so excited over the tiniest things—stickers, bubbles, those little stamp pads that somehow end up all over their hands.

But with balloons, I’ve started kind of… handing things off. Like if there’s a normal classroom celebration and balloons are involved, I’ll ask one of the aides to take over that part or be the one closer to it. And there was this festival art table I had actually planned and was looking forward to, but there were balloons around, and I ended up not helping with it the way I was supposed to.

My supervisor noticed, which was embarrassing. Not in a mean way, but she noticed. So yes, I guess it’s started affecting relationships a little, or at least how reliable I seem at work.
Have you experienced anxiety or fear in situations unrelated to balloons?

I don’t think so… not in the same kind of way. I mean, I can get stressed, sure—like if the classroom schedule gets completely thrown off, or if three kids need help with coats at the exact same time and someone’s crying because they can’t find their mitten. That kind of thing can make me frazzled.

But it’s not like the balloon feeling. I’m trying to think if there’s anything else that makes me feel that same sort of scared, like I need to get away from it, and… I can’t really come up with anything. Sudden noise might startle me, but I don’t go around worrying about it the way I do with balloons.
Do you think you could ever become comfortable being around balloons again, or do you think this fear will always be a problem for you?

I’m not really sure. Part of me wants to say yes, because I feel kind of silly imagining that I’ll be a grown woman forever avoiding balloons, you know? Especially working with little kids—balloons are just sort of everywhere at birthdays and school events.

But then when I actually picture standing near one, especially one that’s tight or squeaky, I don’t feel very confident. I start thinking about how kids grab at them or sit on them, and then I remember one of my students once tried to decorate a balloon with markers and it made that awful rubbing sound—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

I guess I hope I could get more comfortable someday. I don’t know if it’ll always be a problem. Right now it feels hard to imagine it not bothering me.
Do you think your fear of balloons would have developed if the balloon hadn't burst near your face that one time?

I don’t know… I’ve wondered that. I mean, before that happened, balloons weren’t my favorite thing exactly, but I wasn’t planning my day around avoiding them or anything.

It really seems like it started after that one burst close to my face during the children’s art celebration. That was about seven months ago now, I think. Which is strange, because that whole event was supposed to be cute—we had little paint stations and paper crowns, and one child got glitter absolutely everywhere, like in his socks somehow.

But yes, I think if that balloon hadn’t popped right near me, maybe this wouldn’t have become such a thing. Since then it’s just… stuck with me.

target_item.manifestation: I know a balloon in the classroom is probably just decoration, but when I see one stretched tight or bobbing near the children, it feels like it could burst right in my face and I get scared in a way that seems bigger than the situation.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the balloon-specific fear is the primary source of distress rather than a broader anxiety issue, which directly relates to the specific phobic fear.

patient.answer:
I think the balloon thing is the main one, honestly. I mean, everyone gets overwhelmed sometimes, especially with a classroom full of little kids and someone spilling paint or crying because their shoe feels “wrong”—that happens all the time.

But this feels different. Like, I know a balloon in the classroom is probably just decoration, or for a birthday or whatever, but when I see one stretched tight or bobbing around near the children, it feels like it could burst right in my face. And then I get scared in a way that feels… bigger than the situation, if that makes sense.

So yes, I’d say the balloons are the thing that really sets me off more than anything else.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's reaction to balloons is impacting their daily life and relationships
doctor.question: Has your fear of balloons affected your relationships with your students, colleagues, or family members?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It has started affecting my work because I have to hand off normal classroom celebrations to aides and I missed helping with a festival art table I had planned, which my supervisor noticed.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the balloon fear has affected interpersonal functioning with students, colleagues, or family, which is most directly about impairment in functioning.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think it has, mostly at work. I try not to let it show with the kids, because they’re little and they get so excited about birthdays and class celebrations, and I don’t want to be the teacher who ruins that. I mean, they already get so excited over the tiniest things—stickers, bubbles, those little stamp pads that somehow end up all over their hands.

But with balloons, I’ve started kind of… handing things off. Like if there’s a normal classroom celebration and balloons are involved, I’ll ask one of the aides to take over that part or be the one closer to it. And there was this festival art table I had actually planned and was looking forward to, but there were balloons around, and I ended up not helping with it the way I was supposed to.

My supervisor noticed, which was embarrassing. Not in a mean way, but she noticed. So yes, I guess it’s started affecting relationships a little, or at least how reliable I seem at work.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's reaction to balloons is a specific phobia or part of a broader anxiety disorder
doctor.question: Have you experienced anxiety or fear in situations unrelated to balloons?

target_item.reason: The question asks about anxiety or fear in situations unrelated to balloons, but the symptom profile only covers balloon-specific phobic fear and its related impairment/duration.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not in the same kind of way. I mean, I can get stressed, sure—like if the classroom schedule gets completely thrown off, or if three kids need help with coats at the exact same time and someone’s crying because they can’t find their mitten. That kind of thing can make me frazzled.

But it’s not like the balloon feeling. I’m trying to think if there’s anything else that makes me feel that same sort of scared, like I need to get away from it, and… I can’t really come up with anything. Sudden noise might startle me, but I don’t go around worrying about it the way I do with balloons.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's reaction to balloons is consistent with a specific phobia
doctor.question: Do you think you could ever become comfortable being around balloons again, or do you think this fear will always be a problem for you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about expectations for future recovery or whether the fear will persist, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. Part of me wants to say yes, because I feel kind of silly imagining that I’ll be a grown woman forever avoiding balloons, you know? Especially working with little kids—balloons are just sort of everywhere at birthdays and school events.

But then when I actually picture standing near one, especially one that’s tight or squeaky, I don’t feel very confident. I start thinking about how kids grab at them or sit on them, and then I remember one of my students once tried to decorate a balloon with markers and it made that awful rubbing sound—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

I guess I hope I could get more comfortable someday. I don’t know if it’ll always be a problem. Right now it feels hard to imagine it not bothering me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's reaction to balloons is related to a specific traumatic event
doctor.question: Do you think your fear of balloons would have developed if the balloon hadn't burst near your face that one time?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about seven months, ever since a balloon burst close to my face during a children’s art celebration.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the fear began because of the incident when a balloon burst near my face, which is covered by the duration/onset item noting it has been going on for about seven months ever since that event.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… I’ve wondered that. I mean, before that happened, balloons weren’t my favorite thing exactly, but I wasn’t planning my day around avoiding them or anything.

It really seems like it started after that one burst close to my face during the children’s art celebration. That was about seven months ago now, I think. Which is strange, because that whole event was supposed to be cute—we had little paint stations and paper crowns, and one child got glitter absolutely everywhere, like in his socks somehow.

But yes, I think if that balloon hadn’t popped right near me, maybe this wouldn’t have become such a thing. Since then it’s just… stuck with me.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms and history are most consistent with a diagnosis of Acute Stress Disorder (F43.0), given the development of symptoms following a specific traumatic event (the balloon bursting near her face) and the presence of avoidance behaviors, hyperarousal, and intrusive thoughts related to the event.
